title: Aurora Health - Incident Postmortem Follow-up
summary: Redwood and Aurora reviewed the May 28 incident where a KV cache eviction and an unexpected autoscaling race caused sustained latency increases and 502 errors for several minutes. The meeting covered root cause, immediate mitigations taken, proposed durability and rollout changes, security/audit questions, and a set of action items and deadlines for both teams.
next_steps: Redwood to share full postmortem doc and timeline (link) by 2027-06-12
Redwood SE to run KV cache durability tests and share results by 2027-06-17
Aurora to approve a short pilot for pre-warmed nodes on Dedicated by 2027-06-20
Schedule disaster recovery / failover runbook table-top on 2027-06-24
Redwood to provide SOC 2 / audit log extracts requested by Aurora security by 2027-06-15

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-06-10 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45 min
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Ruiz (Redwood CSM), Eleanor Park (Aurora VP Eng), Dr. Samir Khan (Aurora SRE), Nadia Gomez (Aurora Security), Alex Reed (Aurora PM)
Shared: Postmortem deck (drive.redwood.com/aurora/postmortem), SOC2 excerpt (link: /redwood/security/soc2.pdf)

00:00 Liam Chen (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll run through the postmortem and next steps, hopefully keep to 45, um uh quick check on timing, does that work for folks?
00:08 Eleanor Park (Aurora): yes good, thanks Liam, appreciate it, we want to focus on three things root cause, what changed to prevent recurrence, and operational followups.
00:18 Liam Chen: perfect, so quick recap: on 2027-05-28 at ~13:04 UTC we saw a spike in 5xxs and also sustained higher p99 latency for about 7 minutes. this was traced to a KV cache eviction storm in one Dedicated pool followed by an autoscaler race and a partial fallback that didn't fully engage because of a routing mismatch.
00:40 Dr. Samir Khan: yeah to add, the eviction coincided with a large batched workload from a customer job and then the cache entries were repopulated slowly causing token-level regen and CPU contention on the nodes. in short, cache miss amplification.
01:05 Maya Patel (Redwood SE): and to clarify from our side, there was also an older kernel selection path on that pool that made repopulation slower; the autoscaler threshold was hit twice and two new nodes came up but they weren't fully warmed so requests still hit the cold KV cache. there was a fallback policy but because the model variant versions didn't match exactly the routing policy didn't kick in cleanly - a mismatch in the variant tag.
01:36 Alex Reed (Aurora PM): just to confirm, you said fallback existed but didn't engage because of a model tag mismatch? that's... concerning, can you explain?
01:44 Maya Patel: yep that's correct, the routing policy checks model version id and region, and in this case the candidate fallback had a slightly different tag (minor semver) — our rollout system should have normalized tags, but it didn't for that pool due to a stale config.
02:05 Eleanor Park: okay so root cause is multifactor: cache eviction + slow kernel path + autoscale timing + routing tag mismatch.
02:12 Liam Chen: yes, multilayered. the immediate mitigation steps we executed: 1) we bumped autoscaler cooldown and added a pre-warm policy for that customer pool, 2) forced a redeploy with normalized variant tags, 3) applied a hotfix to kernel selection so repopulation is faster, and 4) issued a one-time capacity bump while we investigated. those changes removed the immediate risk.
02:45 Dr. Samir Khan: logs show the error window closed after the redeploy and the p99 returned to baseline, thanks for that quick turn.
03:02 Nadia Gomez (Aurora Security): quick security question — during the outage were any customer logs or payloads persisted to disk or left in non-encrypted storage? we need to confirm no data exposure.
03:14 Maya Patel: short answer no, we only use in-memory KV for cache and we did not persist those entries, and all disk writes are encrypted via KMS, but we'll provide the audit slices. note: transcription may have 'K M S' called out oddly in our auto transcript.
03:32 Nadia Gomez: please share the KMS logs and the audit logs for the timeframe, also we need to see the chain of custody for any node we restarted.
03:40 Liam Chen: understood, we'll attach KMS and audit extracts to the postmortem. link will be in the doc.
03:50 Alex Reed: curious about the frequency, is this something that can happen again if we have a heavy batch job? what's the long-term fix?
04:00 Maya Patel: long term we're proposing three changes: 1) KV cache checkpointing so cold-starts are minimized, 2) stronger pre-warm / warm pools for customers with spiky batch loads, and 3) rollout policy hardening so that variant tag normalization is enforced at the control plane. also adding canary checks that exercise the fallback path automatically.
04:30 Eleanor Park: checkpointing sounds good but we have regulatory constraints on cache persistence in our region — will checkpointing store any PII?
04:40 Maya Patel: checkpointing will only persist opaque cache entries that are derived tokens and not customer text, and we can encrypt-at-rest with your KMS keys. we'll coordinate with your security team.
04:56 Nadia Gomez: we need an explicit spec for what checkpointing stores and KMS key access controls; until we review that we can't approve persistence.
05:06 Liam Chen: fair, we'll include that spec.
05:12 Dr. Samir Khan: on the autoscaler: is changing the cooldown the only thing you did? we think dynamic scale policies that consider cache coldness might be better.
05:22 Maya Patel: agreed, we're prototyping a cache-aware autoscaler that accounts for KV miss rate and pre-warm state, not just CPU. for now we increased cooldown and added a short pre-warm period that keeps one node ready for spiky loads.
05:40 Alex Reed: any tradeoffs on cost? pre-warm nodes obviously cost money.
05:45 Liam Chen: yes cost vs latency tradeoff; we proposed keeping a small pre-warm pool for Aurora's high-sensitivity routes and Redwood can absorb a portion as a customer credit for the incident window, then Aurora can choose whether to adopt a paid pre-warm SLA. we'll put numbers in the postmortem doc.
06:10 Eleanor Park: please highlight what we need from Aurora to approve the production changes.
06:15 Sofia Ruiz (Redwood CSM): checklist we need from Aurora: confirmation of KMS key for checkpoint encryption, list of routes to mark as high-sensitivity, and access to recent logs for repro. we'll include this in the action items.
06:32 Liam Chen: quick note about observability — we added additional tracing hooks and a dedicated alert on KV miss rate crossing 30% for more than 30s. that alert will page SRE and Redwood ops.
06:48 Dr. Samir Khan: good, can you make the alert send the specific tenant id and last 5 request IDs? that'll speed debugging.
06:56 Maya Patel: yep we can include tenant id and last request ids, but we have to be careful with PII in alerts; we'll strip any payloads.
07:15 Alex Reed: what about the fallback not engaging — can the control plane simulate the fallback periodically so we know it will work in prod?
07:24 Maya Patel: good idea, we can add automated canary tests that force mismatched tags and run a smoke check, and we also have a rollback policy to fallback to a compatible model variant.
07:38 Eleanor Park: timeline for fixes? we need approximate dates for the kernel fix, checkpoint PoC, and rollout normalization.
07:45 Liam Chen: kernel hotfix already rolled on 2027-05-29; checkpoint PoC we'll deliver mid-June (Maya target 2027-06-17), rollout normalization changes and control-plane guardrails targeted for 2027-06-20.
08:02 Nadia Gomez: we'll review the PoC for checkpointing before any persistence is enabled. also we expect SOC2 artifacts as part of the postmortem packet.
08:12 Sofia Ruiz: we'll include the SOC2 slice. link in the postmortem doc.
08:20 Alex Reed: any other permanent reliability improvements you're proposing?
08:23 Maya Patel: also adding KV eviction backpressure — so the runtime will pause low-priority repopulation if CPU or mem crosses a threshold, and prioritize critical routes. plus better circuit breaking so heavy batch jobs can't starve inference.
08:45 Eleanor Park: that sounds reasonable. we'll want to see the circuit-breaker rules and test results.
08:52 Liam Chen: yes we'll share the proposed rules and test logs.
09:00 Dr. Samir Khan: on the testing side, can Redwood run a scaled repro test that mirrors our internal batch workload? we can share the job parameters.
09:10 Maya Patel: absolutely, we'll run the repro in Redwood's staging cluster with Aurora's traces (sanitized) and share metrics. schedule the test window?
09:18 Alex Reed: how long does that typically take?
09:20 Maya Patel: a 2-4 hour run plus analysis, we can do an overnight run and have results next day.
09:28 Liam Chen: to recap next steps and ownership... (recap then timestamps)
09:40 Liam Chen: we'll attach postmortem doc, SOC2 excerpt, KMS/audit slices; Redwood to run KV durability tests; Aurora to provide logs and KMS key details; we'll schedule the tabletop DR.
10:05 Eleanor Park: sounds good, one ask: can Redwood provide a one-time credit for the customer impact window?
10:12 Liam Chen: yes, we proposed a goodwill credit; exact amount in the postmortem.
10:20 Alex Reed: timeline wise when will we see the doc and the tests?
10:24 Liam Chen: postmortem doc by 2027-06-12, KV tests results by 2027-06-17, DR tabletop week of 2027-06-24.
10:40 Nadia Gomez: thanks. we'll review and revert with any compliance blockers.
10:46 Sofia Ruiz: thanks all, we'll follow up in writing with the links and schedule.
10:52 Meeting ends

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis-transcribed acronyms (e.g. "sock two" for SOC2, "sam-el" for SAML) due to auto-captions. All artifacts will be provided as links in the postmortem doc.
